title: Ascariasis
path: Prevention and Control of Communicable Diseases

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Ascariasis
headings.content: Ascariasis is one of the most common human parasitic worm infections globally, predominantly affecting populations in tropical and subtropical regions with inadequate sanitation and hygiene infrastructure, such as various communities in Nigeria. It is caused by the giant roundworm, Ascaris lumbricoides. As student nurses preparing for clinical practice and professional examinations under the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria, understanding this infection is crucial because it heavily impacts pediatric health, nutritional status, and growth. The parasite primarily inhabits the lumen of the small intestine, where adult worms can live for up to two years, competing with the host for essential nutrients. While many light infections are asymptomatic, heavy worm burdens can lead to severe nutritional deficiencies, growth stunting in children, and life-threatening surgical emergencies like intestinal obstruction. Ascariasis is a major neglected tropical disease closely linked to poverty, lack of clean potable water, and poor waste disposal systems. Recognizing the socio-economic and environmental determinants of ascariasis allows nurses to design holistic care plans that address both the clinical symptoms and the underlying community health deficits. Public health campaigns spearheaded by nurses often target school-aged children, who represent the demographic with the highest prevalence and intensity of infection, making early identification and community-wide education vital components of professional nursing care in Nigeria.

headings.title: Etiology and the Life Cycle of Ascaris lumbricoides
headings.content: Ascaris lumbricoides is a large nematode whose complex life cycle involves both the human host and the external environment. Adult female worms residing in the small intestine produce hundreds of thousands of eggs daily, which are passed out in human feces. These unembryonated eggs require a period of weeks in warm, moist, shaded soil to develop into the infectious embryonated stage containing a second-stage larva. Infection occurs when a human accidentally ingests these infective eggs, usually through contaminated food, water, or soil-soiled hands (fecal-oral route). Once swallowed, the eggs hatch in the small intestine, releasing larvae that penetrate the intestinal mucosa. The larvae then enter the venous circulation or lymphatics, traveling to the liver and subsequently to the heart and lungs. In the pulmonary capillaries, the larvae break out into the alveoli, causing a transient inflammatory reaction. They ascend the bronchial tree to the pharynx, where they are swallowed a second time. Upon reaching the small intestine once more, the larvae mature into adult male and female worms, completing the cycle. Understanding this intricate migration path through the hepatic and pulmonary systems is essential for nurses to connect early respiratory symptoms like coughing to a parasitic etiology before intestinal manifestations become prominent.

headings.title: Mode of Transmission and Risk Factors in Nigerian Communities
headings.content: The transmission of ascariasis is intimately tied to environmental sanitation, personal hygiene practices, and agricultural methods. In many Nigerian communities, the practice of open defecation or the use of untreated human excreta (night soil) as fertilizer for vegetable farming heavily contaminates the soil with Ascaris eggs. Because these eggs have a tough outer shell, they can survive in harsh soil environments for years, waiting for a susceptible host. Transmission primarily occurs via the fecal-oral route when individuals consume unwashed raw vegetables, fruits grown in contaminated soil, or unpotable water containing infective eggs. Poor hand hygiene after handling soil or before eating is a major risk factor, particularly among children who play outdoors and engage in geophagia (eating soil). Sub-optimal community infrastructure, such as a lack of safe piped water systems and inadequate sewage disposal, further perpetuates transmission cycles. For nursing students, recognizing these community-level risk factors is critical for formulating effective health education initiatives. Nurses must emphasize the importance of thorough vegetable washing, safe water consumption, proper handwashing with soap, and the construction and utilization of sanitary latrines to interrupt the transmission cycle in endemic areas.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations
headings.content: The pathophysiology of ascariasis depends heavily on the phase of the parasite's life cycle and the total worm burden. During the early migratory phase through the lungs, larval migration can trigger a hypersensitivity reaction characterized by eosinophilic pneumonitis, cough, wheezing, and dyspnea, a clinical presentation known as Löffler's syndrome. Once the worms establish residency in the small intestine, light infections are typically asymptomatic. However, moderate to heavy worm burdens cause direct pathological effects. Adult worms physically compete with the host for vital nutrients, leading to protein-energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiencies, and iron-deficiency anemia, which gravely impairs childhood growth and cognitive development. Furthermore, the sheer physical presence and mobility of adult worms can lead to mechanical irritation of the intestinal mucosa, vague abdominal pain, nausea, and anorexia. In severe cases, a tangled mass of worms can cause complete mechanical intestinal obstruction, intussusception, or volvulus. Wandering adult worms can also migrate aberrantly into the biliary tree, pancreatic duct, or appendix, causing acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, pancreatitis, or appendicitis. Recognizing these diverse clinical manifestations helps nurses anticipate complications and monitor patients closely for acute abdominal emergencies.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Nursing assessment for a patient with suspected ascariasis begins with a thorough health history and physical examination. The nurse should inquire about travel history, living conditions, access to clean water, sanitation practices, and dietary habits such as consuming unwashed vegetables. During the physical examination, the nurse assesses for signs of malnutrition, growth stunting, abdominal distension, tenderness, and altered bowel sounds. Respiratory assessments are vital if the patient presents with early migratory symptoms like a persistent dry cough and wheezing. The cornerstone of definitive diagnostic evaluation is stool microscopy, where the characteristic fertilized or unfertilized eggs of Ascaris lumbricoides are identified via saline mount or concentration techniques. In light infections with only male worms, stool examination may be negative because no eggs are produced; thus, clinical history remains critical. Occasionally, adult worms may be spontaneously passed in the stool or vomited, which serves as an obvious diagnostic indicator. In emergency scenarios involving severe complications, imaging studies such as abdominal plain films or ultrasounds may reveal the presence of worm masses, intestinal obstruction, or biliary tree involvement. Laboratory tests may show peripheral eosinophilia during the pulmonary migration phase and microcytic anemia resulting from chronic nutritional compromise.

headings.title: Medical Management and Pharmacological Treatment
headings.content: Medical management of ascariasis focuses on eradicating the parasite using safe, effective, and well-tolerated anthelmintic medications. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends single-dose regimens of benzimidazoles, such as albendazole (400 mg orally) or mebendazole (100 mg twice daily for three days or a single 500 mg dose), as first-line treatments. Alternatively, ivermectin or pyrantel pamoate are used depending on clinical guidelines and patient profile. These drugs work by impairing glucose uptake in the parasite or causing neuromuscular paralysis, leading to the expulsion of the worms from the gastrointestinal tract. Nurses play a crucial role in administering these medications, educating patients on potential mild side effects such as transient abdominal discomfort or nausea, and monitoring for effective passage of worms. In cases of severe complications like intestinal obstruction or biliary ascariasis, medical management must shift rapidly from simple anthelmintic therapy. Anthelmintic drugs may sometimes be deferred during acute complete obstruction to avoid stimulating worm motility that could worsen blockage or perforation; surgical intervention or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) may be urgently required to relieve the obstruction before pharmacological deworming is safely resumed.

headings.title: Complications of Severe Ascariasis
headings.content: While many individuals experience mild or asymptomatic ascariasis, heavy infections can precipitate severe, life-threatening complications that demand urgent multidisciplinary medical and surgical intervention. The most common surgical emergency is mechanical intestinal obstruction, typically occurring in young children with heavy worm loads. The bolus of dead or motile worms creates a physical blockage, leading to severe colicky abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and potential bowel ischemia, necrosis, or perforation. Another serious complication arises when adult worms migrate aberrantly into adjacent structures. Migration into the biliary tree can cause acute biliary colic, cholecystitis, acute cholangitis, or pyogenic liver abscesses. If worms enter the pancreatic duct, they can trigger acute pancreatitis. In pediatric populations, heavy infections severely compromise nutritional status, contributing to chronic protein-energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiencies, and iron-deficiency anemia, which collectively result in growth stunting, physical weakness, and cognitive deficits. Nurses must maintain a high index of suspicion for these complications, monitoring vital signs, abdominal girth, bowel sounds, and pain levels closely to ensure prompt escalation of care when emergency surgical or endoscopic intervention is indicated.

headings.title: Community Health Nursing Interventions, Prevention, and Control
headings.content: Community health nursing plays a pivotal role in the prevention and control of ascariasis, particularly in endemic rural and semi-urban settings across Nigeria. Because reinfection is common after individual treatment, community-wide and school-based mass drug administration (MDA) programs are key strategies supported by public health nurses and international health agencies. Nurses organize and execute periodic deworming campaigns targeting school-aged children and preschool-age children to reduce overall community worm burden and improve nutritional outcomes. Beyond pharmacotherapy, sustainable control relies heavily on health education and environmental sanitation improvements. Community health nurses conduct outreach programs to educate populations on proper hand hygiene—especially washing hands with soap before eating and after handling soil—and the safe preparation of food, including washing raw vegetables thoroughly with clean water. Nurses also advocate for and educate communities on the construction and proper use of sanitary latrines to prevent open defecation and subsequent soil contamination. Collaboration with local leaders, environmental health officers, and governmental bodies to ensure access to safe, potable drinking water is an essential nursing intervention. Through comprehensive education and sanitation advocacy, nurses empower communities to break the cycle of transmission and achieve long-term health resilience against parasitic infections.
